title: edge-nat-scaling-and-egress-strategy-tf-sketch
content:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch for a robust egress (NAT) and edge-networking strategy for Private deployments (VPC + on-prem hybrid). Focus is on scaling NAT capacity for bursty model-serving traffic, minimizing per-token latency impact, preserving private DNS semantics, and enabling Terraform-driven upgrades with safe rollbacks.

Goals:
- Provide elastic, low-latency egress for tenant workloads while enforcing per-tenant firewall/egress rules.
- Keep private DNS (split-horizon) intact for internal services and model registry lookups during upgrades.
- Make Terraform modules composable and idempotent for NAT pools, IP rotation, and firewall policy rollout.
- Offer clear upgrade path (canary -> staggered -> full) with automated validation and rollback.

Constraints & assumptions:
- Customers may be in cloud VPCs or air-gapped on-prem racks with egress proxies.
- Some deployments require static egress IPs for allowlists; others allow ephemeral pooled IPs.
- K8s clusters use Calico network policies (default), but we must support iptables-based clusters too.
- TLS termination may be upstream; we must avoid TLS inspection in path unless explicitly enabled.

High-level architecture options (tradeoffs):
1) NAT Gateway Pool (preferred for hosted-like VPCs)
   - Managed pool of NAT gateways (cloud-NAT-style) or on-prem HA NAT appliances.
   - Route-based failover to healthy NAT instances.
   - Good for static egress IP requirements (assign reserved IPs to pool).
   - Downside: capacity planning required; bursty workloads need autoscaling.

2) Egress Proxy Fleet (Envoy/HAProxy) + SNAT at edge
   - Sidecar-less: cluster egress routed to a proxy fleet in the edge VPC; proxies perform TLS origination/forwarding.
   - Flexible controls (per-tenant headers, auth), easier to inject QC and telemetry.
   - If proxies are stateful, need sticky hashing; scale with k8s autoscaling groups.

3) Hybrid: local SNAT + central proxy for allowlist/inspection customers
   - Default path: SNAT at node-level or gateway (lower latency).
   - Special-case: route selected tenants through proxy fleet for observability/compliance.

Terraform module notes (patterns and recommended inputs):
- Module: redwood_private_nat_pool
  inputs (strings/lists): name, vpc_id, region, subnet_ids, desired_pool_size, nat_type (managed|proxy|onprem), static_ips (optional list), scale_policy (min,max,cpu_threshold), healthcheck_endpoint, tagging_map
  outputs: pool_id, ip_addresses (list), route_table_ids, health_status
  behaviors: when nat_type=managed, create cloud NAT resources; when onprem, generate expected BGP/route config templates and a plan artifact for ops.
  lifecycle: use create_before_destroy for NAT instances that change allocation to avoid transient egress failures.

- Module: redwood_egress_firewall
  inputs: tenant_id, allowed_destinations (CIDR list or fqdn patterns), deny_by_default (bool), logging_bucket, alerting_webhook
  recommended pattern: generate per-tenant firewall policy resources and a global fallback deny rule.

- Module: redwood_split_horizon_dns
  inputs: zone_name, forwarders (list), internal_records (map as encoded string), ttl_default, conditional_forwarders (for onprem service meshes)
  notes: store glue records for private endpoints and ensure forwarders are healthchecked; support DNS-over-TLS forwarders where required.

Upgrade plan (NAT pool expansion / replacement):
- Prep: ensure terraform plan has NO resource replacement for route tables unless explicitly intended. Verify module uses create_before_destroy for NAT instances.
- Canary phase (small % of nodes/tenants):
  1) Deploy new NAT instance(s) with reserved IPs alongside existing pool.
  2) Update route priorities or attach subset of subnets to new NAT (use tagging to pick canary subnets).
  3) Run synthetic traffic tests: large prompt generation, streaming checks, DNS resolution tests against private zones.
  4) Monitor egress latency, error rates, and per-IP connection limits.
  5) If failures: revert subnet route to previous NAT and drain the failing instance.
- Staggered rollout: progressively shift more subnets/tenant routes over in waves (1 hour apart), validating healthchecks and DNS lookups after each wave.
- Full rollout: once stable, move routing tables to reference new NAT pool and decommission old instances with drain period.

Rollback plan:
- Terraform apply that reverts route attachment to prior NAT pool (keep old pool until new one passes full validation).
- If route replacement was destructive, use reserved IPs to rebind to previous instance.
- Update SRE runbook with steps: check route tables, SGs, NAT health endpoints, and re-enable previous firewall rules.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-merge & pre-rollout):
- Terraform plan review: ensure no unexpected deletions, confirm create_before_destroy on NAT instances.
- Unit tests: tfvalidate + tflint rules for naming and tag requirements.
- Integration smoke: curl to internal model registry, fetch embeddings endpoint, simulate 1k concurrent short requests and 50 concurrent long streaming sessions.
- DNS tests: resolve private names from both kube and host namespaces; test fallback forwarders.
- Egress IP verification: confirm source IPs for test flows match expected static or pooled addresses.
- Policy test: enforce deny-by-default and verify allowed destination whitelists function per-tenant.

Firewall & network policy considerations:
- Cloud firewall rules: order matters. Ensure explicit allow rules for management/control-plane IP ranges before global denies.
- K8s NetworkPolicy templates (namespace-level): provide base templates that allow egress to NAT pool IPs and to internal registries but deny broad internet egress unless tenant policy allows.
- Masquerade vs preserve-source: when preserving client IP is important (for external allowlists), use externalTrafficPolicy=Local for ingress and avoid node SNAT; if using SNAT, ensure downstream services expect pooled source IPs.

Operational runbook snippets (commands and checks):
- Check active NAT instance health: curl -f http://10.10.10.1:8080/health || echo "NAT unhealthy"
- Verify routes attached to subnet: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=tag:Name,Values="redwood-nat-*"
- Validate DNS forwarders: dig @10.1.2.3 private-svc.internal +short
- Rotate static egress IP (cloud): 1) allocate new Elastic IPs, 2) attach to new NAT, 3) switch route table target to new NAT, 4) verify allowlists.

Open questions / risks:
- Connection tracking limits: some NAT appliances have per-CPU conntrack constraints. We need telemetry to detect conntrack saturation and autoscale before reach.
- Packet-per-second (PPS) vs connection limits for token-heavy streaming workloads—need load tests.
- On-prem fallbacks for air-gapped installs: how to gracefully degrade when external model endpoint is unreachable? (local mirror? cached model blobs?)
- Compliance: for some customers we must avoid third-party managed proxies. Make sure module supports entirely customer-managed appliances.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Create a terraform submodule PR with skeleton for redwood_private_nat_pool (owner: Liam). See github.com/redwood-inference/infra-private/pull/84 for initial branch.
- Add conntrack and PPS alarms to observability dashboards (owner: Priya).
- Draft customer runbook for static IP rotation and allowlist change (owner: Mateo).
- Schedule lab load test (1M tokens/hour sustained) against canary NAT to measure latencies and conntrack behavior.

Notes-to-self: keep minimal path for low-latency egress (avoid proxy for default) but ship a proxy path for customers who want header enrichment and per-request RBAC. Keep Terraform modules small and composable (one responsibility per module).

References and links:
- INF-2317: NAT scaling proposal and benchmarks (Jira)
- github.com/redwood-inference/infra-private/pull/84 (module skeleton)
- internal slack thread: #private-deployments - thread ts 1702012345

End of sketch.
